source: NCERT India and the Contemporary World II (Class X History), Chapter II

overview.bigIdea: In India nationalism grew out of the **struggle against colonialism**. Gandhiji’s **satyagraha** drew peasants, tribals, workers, women and businessmen into one movement – but each group meant something different by **swaraj**, so unity was real yet fragile: ‘a nation with many voices’.

ladder.a: War hardship, satyagraha, Rowlatt, Jallianwalla Bagh
Simon, Purna Swaraj, Salt March, Civil Disobedience
Peasants, business, workers, women; dalits and Muslims lukewarm

ladder.q: How did people feel one nation?

languages.name: Groups

languages.name: Symbols
languages.text: Bharat Mata, flags and folklore for ‘collective belonging’.

plan.text: Lesson 1 – war, satyagraha, Rowlatt, Jallianwalla Bagh, Khilafat.
Lesson 2 – Non-Cooperation in towns, countryside, plantations (sort activity).
Lessons 3–4 – Simon to Salt March; how groups saw the movement.
Lesson 5, then the quiz; revise after 1, 3 and 7 days.

lessons.title: War, satyagraha and the Rowlatt Act
lessons.hook: Prices doubled, villages had to give soldiers, crops failed and **12–13 million** people died of famine and influenza. People hoped hardship would end after the war. It did not – and a new leader offered a new way to fight: **satyagraha**.

core.def: Defence spending financed by war loans and taxes (customs duties raised, income tax introduced); prices doubled 1913–1918; forced recruitment; famines and influenza.
Power of truth: if the cause is true, physical force is unnecessary; win by non-violence by appealing to the oppressor’s conscience.
Champaran 1917 (plantation system), Kheda 1918 (revenue), Ahmedabad 1918 (cotton mill workers).
Gave enormous powers to repress political activity; detention without trial for two years; hartal on 6 April.
13 April 1919, Amritsar; General Dyer blocked exits and fired, killing hundreds, to ‘produce a moral effect’.
Committee formed in Bombay, March 1919 (Muhammad Ali and Shaukat Ali) to defend the Khalifa; Gandhiji used it to unite Hindus and Muslims.

explain: **Repression:** satyagrahis were forced to rub noses on the ground, crawl and salute sahibs; villages around Gujranwala were bombed. Gandhiji called off the Rowlatt satyagraha as violence spread.
**Broadening:** the Rowlatt movement was mostly urban; Gandhiji wanted a broad-based movement and Hindu–Muslim unity – hence Khilafat and Non-Cooperation (Calcutta, September 1920).

example.q: How did the First World War help in the growth of the national movement in India? (3 marks)
steps: **Economic hardship:** defence expenditure financed by war loans and higher taxes – customs duties raised, income tax introduced.
**Prices:** doubled between 1913 and 1918, causing extreme hardship.
**Forced recruitment** in villages caused widespread anger; crop failures and influenza killed 12–13 million (census 1921). People’s anger made them ready for a mass movement.
example.answer: Taxes, prices, forced recruitment and famine – anger that fed the movement.

mistakes: Dating Jallianwalla Bagh to 6 April (that was the hartal; the massacre was 13 April).
lessons.tip: Rowlatt answers: what the Act did (detention without trial) + why Indians were outraged (passed despite united Indian opposition).
lessons.memory: 1915 return · 1917 Champaran · 1918 Kheda & Ahmedabad · 1919 Rowlatt, 13 April Jallianwalla, Khilafat Committee.

lessons.title: Non-Cooperation and its differing strands
lessons.hook: ‘If Indians refuse to cooperate, British rule will collapse within a year.’ In **January 1921** students left schools, lawyers left courts and foreign cloth burned – while peasants, tribals and tea-garden workers each heard **swaraj** in their own way.

core.def: Surrender titles; boycott civil services, army, police, courts, councils, schools and foreign goods; civil disobedience if repressed.
Students, teachers, lawyers joined; councils boycotted except Madras (Justice Party); foreign cloth imports fell from Rs 102 crore to Rs 57 crore.
Baba Ramchandra; against talukdars’ high rents, cesses and begar; nai–dhobi bandhs; Oudh Kisan Sabha (Oct 1920) with Nehru; 300 branches.
Alluri Sitaram Raju; forest closure and forced begar; guerrilla war; executed 1924.
Inland Emigration Act 1859; workers left gardens for home, believing Gandhi Raj was coming; stranded and beaten.

explain: **Why it slowed in towns:** khadi cost more than mill cloth; Indian alternative institutions were slow to come up.
**Different meanings:** the visions of these groups were not defined by the Congress programme, yet acting in Gandhiji’s name linked them to an all-India agitation.

example.q: List the social groups which joined Non-Cooperation. Choose three and explain why they joined. (5 marks)
steps: **Groups:** urban middle class (students, teachers, lawyers), merchants, peasants of Awadh, tribals of Gudem Hills, Assam plantation workers.
**Middle class:** answered the call for swaraj – left government schools and courts, boycotted councils and foreign cloth.
**Awadh peasants:** against talukdars’ high rents, cesses and begar; wanted revenue cut and social boycott of landlords.
**Gudem tribals:** forests closed and begar for roads; Raju led guerrilla war for swaraj.
**Plantation workers:** wanted freedom to leave the gardens and return to their villages.
example.answer: Name all groups, then three detailed with their grievance and meaning of swaraj.

mistakes: Saying Madras boycotted the council elections.
Calling Alluri Sitaram Raju a non-violent satyagrahi.
Forgetting why the city movement slowed down.
lessons.tip: Make a 3-column table – Group · Grievance · What swaraj meant. It answers most questions on this lesson.
lessons.memory: Nagpur Dec 1920 · Jan 1921 start · Rs 102 → 57 crore · Ramchandra (Awadh), Raju (Gudem), 1859 Act (Assam).

lessons.title: Towards Civil Disobedience and the Salt March
lessons.hook: On **6 April 1930** at Dandi, Gandhiji picked up salt made by boiling sea water. A tiny act – but it told millions: break unjust laws, peacefully.

core.def: Chauri Chaura violence; Swaraj Party (C. R. Das, Motilal Nehru) for council politics; Nehru and Bose for radical mass agitation and full independence.
Depression – farm prices fell from 1926, collapsed after 1930; Simon Commission (no Indian member), arrived 1928, ‘Go back Simon’.
Lahore Congress, December 1929, under Nehru; 26 January 1930 Independence Day.
31 Jan 1930 letter with 11 demands; ultimatum till 11 March; 78 volunteers; 240 miles in 24 days; Sabarmati to Dandi; salt law broken 6 April.
Ghaffar Khan arrested (Peshawar); Sholapur workers; about 100,000 arrested; Gandhi-Irwin Pact 5 March 1931; 2nd Round Table Conference Dec 1931 fails; relaunch 1932; lost momentum by 1934.

explain: **What was new:** people were asked not only to refuse cooperation but to **break colonial laws** – salt law, forest laws, refusing revenue and chaukidari taxes; officials resigned.
**Revolutionaries (Box 1):** HSRA founded 1928 in Delhi – Bhagat Singh, Jatin Das, Ajoy Ghosh; bomb in the Legislative Assembly (April 1929); Bhagat Singh executed at 23.

example.q: Discuss the Salt March to make clear why it was an effective symbol of resistance against colonialism. (5 marks)
steps: **Universal item:** salt was consumed by rich and poor alike – one of the most essential foods.
**Oppression made visible:** the tax and government monopoly showed the most oppressive face of British rule.
**Mobilisation:** 240 miles in 24 days with 78 volunteers; thousands came to listen at every stop.
**Mass law-breaking:** on 6 April 1930 Gandhiji made salt at Dandi; thousands broke the salt law across India.
**Spread:** it started the Civil Disobedience Movement – boycotts, picketing, refusal of taxes, forest laws violated.

mistakes: Saying the Simon Commission had Indian members.
Mixing up Lahore 1929 (Purna Swaraj) with Nagpur 1920 (Non-Cooperation).
Writing that the Salt March began on 6 April (that was the day salt was made at Dandi).
lessons.tip: For ‘how was CDM different from NCM’, use one sentence: NCM = refuse to cooperate; CDM = refuse AND break laws.
lessons.memory: 1922 Chauri Chaura · 1928 Simon · Dec 1929 Lahore · 26 Jan 1930 · 6 Apr 1930 Dandi · 5 Mar 1931 Pact · 1932 relaunch.
examAsk: Why was the Simon Commission opposed?

How was Civil Disobedience different from Non-Cooperation?

lessons.title: How participants saw the movement and its limits
lessons.hook: A Patidar farmer, a Birla, a Nagpur mill worker, a woman picketing a liquor shop, a dalit leader and a Muslim League member – all heard ‘swaraj’, but each wanted something different.

core.def: Patidars (Gujarat), Jats (UP); hit by depression; swaraj = lower revenue; disappointed in 1931.
Small tenants wanted unpaid rent remitted; joined Socialist/Communist movements; Congress avoided ‘no rent’ campaigns.
Indian Industrial and Commercial Congress (1920), FICCI (1927); Thakurdas, Birla; wanted protection and a favourable rupee-sterling ratio; cooled after the Round Table failed.
Mostly aloof except Nagpur; railway strikes 1930, dockworkers 1932, Chotanagpur tin miners in Gandhi caps.
Joined marches, made salt, picketed; high-caste urban and rich-peasant rural families; Congress gave only symbolic roles.
Ambedkar – Depressed Classes Association 1930, separate electorates; Poona Pact Sept 1932. Muslims alienated after Khilafat; separate electorates dispute; Iqbal 1930.

explain: **Poona Pact:** reserved seats for the Depressed Classes in provincial and central councils, but voted in by the general electorate.
**Communal distrust:** Congress linked with groups like the Hindu Mahasabha; riots; 1927 unity talks; Jinnah’s offer; Jayakar’s opposition at the 1928 All Parties Conference.

example.q: Why did political leaders differ sharply over the question of separate electorates? (5 marks)
steps: **Dalit leaders (Ambedkar):** political empowerment through separate electorates and reserved seats would end social disabilities.
**Gandhiji:** separate electorates would slow down dalits’ integration into society; fast unto death; Poona Pact 1932.
**Muslim leaders (Iqbal, 1930):** separate electorates were a safeguard for a minority facing economic inferiority, debt and insufficient majorities.
**Jinnah’s offer:** give up separate electorates if assured reserved seats in the Central Assembly and proportional representation in Bengal and Punjab.
**Hindu Mahasabha:** M. R. Jayakar opposed compromise at the 1928 All Parties Conference – distrust grew.
example.answer: Present each side: dalits, Gandhiji, Muslim leaders, Hindu Mahasabha.

mistakes: Saying the Poona Pact gave dalits separate electorates (it gave reserved seats with a general electorate).
Saying all business groups supported Congress throughout.
Writing that women got leadership posts in the Congress.
lessons.tip: Each group: WHO + WHY JOINED + WHAT SWARAJ MEANT + LIMIT. Four lines per group = full marks.
lessons.memory: Patidars & Jats · FICCI 1927 · Nagpur workers · Ambedkar 1930 · Poona Pact Sept 1932 · Iqbal 1930.

lessons.title: The sense of collective belonging
lessons.hook: How does a nation become real in people’s minds? Not only through struggle – also through a **mother figure**, folk songs, a flag carried in a march, and a proud story of the past.

core.def: Created by Bankim Chandra (Vande Mataram, 1870s; Anandamath); Abanindranath Tagore’s 1905 painting – calm, ascetic, dispensing learning, food, clothing; later forms with trishul, lion and elephant.
Rabindranath Tagore collected ballads, nursery rhymes and myths; Natesa Sastri’s The Folklore of Southern India – folklore as national literature.
Swadeshi tricolour (red, green, yellow) – eight lotuses, crescent moon; Swaraj flag 1921 (red, green, white) with spinning wheel.
Nationalist histories showed a glorious ancient past and decline under colonialism to instil pride.
Wardha resolution 14 July 1942; AICC Bombay 8 August 1942; ‘Do or Die’; Jayprakash Narayan, Aruna Asaf Ali, Ram Manohar Lohia; Matangini Hazra, Kanaklata Barua, Rama Devi.

explain: **Problem:** when the past glorified was Hindu and images came from Hindu iconography, other communities felt left out.
**Conclusion:** Congress tried to resolve differences, but unity often broke down – ‘a nation with many voices wanting freedom’.

example.q: How did cultural processes help create a sense of collective belonging? (5 marks)
steps: **Image of the nation:** Bharat Mata by Bankim Chandra; Abanindranath Tagore’s painting; devotion to her seen as nationalism.
**Songs:** ‘Vande Mataram’ sung widely during the Swadeshi movement.
**Folklore:** Tagore and Natesa Sastri collected folk tales to recover national identity and pride.
**Flags:** Swadeshi tricolour and Gandhiji’s Swaraj flag – carrying it became a symbol of defiance.
**History:** reinterpreted to show past glory and inspire struggle; but Hindu imagery made some communities feel left out.
example.answer: Image, song, folklore, flags, history – plus one limitation.

mistakes: Saying Abanindranath Tagore wrote Vande Mataram.
Mixing up the two flags’ colours and symbols.
lessons.tip: Compare Bharat Mata with Germania (Chapter I): both are female allegories of the nation – a common exam question.
lessons.memory: Bankim 1870s · Abanindranath 1905 · Swaraj flag 1921 (spinning wheel) · Quit India 8 Aug 1942.

revision: Indian nationalism grew with the anti-colonial movement; each group felt colonialism differently.
War: taxes and loans, prices doubled 1913–18, forced recruitment, famine and influenza (12–13 million dead).
Satyagraha: truth and non-violence; Champaran 1917, Kheda and Ahmedabad 1918.
Rowlatt Act 1919: detention without trial for 2 years; hartal 6 April; Jallianwalla Bagh 13 April.
Khilafat Committee (Bombay, March 1919); Calcutta Sept 1920; Nagpur Dec 1920 adopts Non-Cooperation.
NCM in towns: boycotts; councils boycotted except Madras; cloth imports Rs 102 → 57 crore; slowed – khadi costly, no alternatives.
Countryside: Baba Ramchandra (Awadh), Oudh Kisan Sabha; Alluri Sitaram Raju (Gudem); Assam workers and the 1859 Act.
Feb 1922 Chauri Chaura → withdrawal; Swaraj Party; depression; Simon Commission 1928.
Lahore Dec 1929 Purna Swaraj; Salt March, Dandi 6 April 1930; CDM = break laws.
Gandhi-Irwin Pact 5 March 1931; 2nd Round Table Dec 1931 fails; relaunch 1932; lost momentum by 1934.
Groups: rich peasants (revenue), poor peasants (rent), business (FICCI 1927), workers (Nagpur), women (symbolic role).
Dalits: Ambedkar 1930; Poona Pact Sept 1932. Muslims: alienated; Iqbal 1930; Jayakar 1928.
Belonging: Bharat Mata, Vande Mataram, folklore, Swadeshi and Swaraj flags, reinterpreted history.
Quit India: Wardha 14 July 1942; Bombay 8 August; ‘Do or Die’.

sections.title: Movement answers · 4 steps
items: Give the date and the trigger.
Show the groups and what swaraj meant to them.
End with why it stopped and what it achieved.

sections.title: Answer writing that scores
items: Start with a one-line introduction using the textbook’s key term (e.g. ‘Proto-industrialisation was …’).
Write in points – one idea per point, key term first. A 3-mark answer needs 3 clear points; a 5-mark answer needs 5.
Add a date, a name or a figure from the chapter to each point – but only when you are sure of it.
For ‘Explain / Analyse’ use PEE: Point → Explain → Example. For ‘Compare’ draw a small two-column table.
Source-based questions: underline the key line in the source first; the answer is usually hidden in it.

sections.title: Before the exam
items: Revise the key facts sheet and the revision list the night before.
Redo the Play & learn timelines and sorts – if you get every card first time, you know the chapter.
Practise one 5-mark answer in 8–10 minutes with a timer.

checklist: I can explain the effects of the First World War and the idea of satyagraha.
I can describe the Rowlatt satyagraha, Jallianwalla Bagh and Khilafat.
I can explain how different groups joined Non-Cooperation and why it was withdrawn.
I can trace events from the Simon Commission to the Gandhi-Irwin Pact.
I can explain how participants saw Civil Disobedience and its limits.
I can explain how a sense of collective belonging was created.
exam.paperNote: Based on the CBSE Class X Social Science pattern (MCQ, assertion–reason, 3-mark short, 4-mark source-based and 5-mark long answers; History also has map work). Practise these types first.

method: Built on proven learning methods: understand the story first, sort and match ideas with your hands (active learning), write model answers point by point, test yourself (active recall) and revisit after 1, 3 and 7 days (spaced revision).
